It's right, isn't it, Mr. Marinkovic, that you told the Investigative Judge that those Muslim soldiers were also named the Mujahedin, so I'm not interested in what their individual names were. But collectively, those local Bosnians were part and parcel of the Mujahedin, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe there is something here, but it wasn't done like that. But in the action, everybody was saying, "Allahu Akbar," and perhaps that's what it was. The Muslims were also saying "Allahu Akbar," so perhaps we thought that all of them were Mujahedin. That's what it could have been, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we can clarify your evidence, and now I'm not interested in the document on the screen in front of you. When you were captured, did you think that all of the men who captured you, both foreigners and local Bosnians, were the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm repeating the same thing again. In the action, when we heard all of them shouting "Allah Ekber," and when the action was, we thought those were the Mujahedin. But then again this is my assumption. I was thinking that the Muslims, too, if they were saying "Allah Ekber," we then could have thought that they were all Mujahedin. Maybe that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you thought that they all could have been Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what -- at least that's what my thinking was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor back in 1999, you told the investigator: "On 21 July, I was captured in a battle by Mujahedin soldiers."

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the men who captured you, they then took you to a village which you've told us is Livade?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You didn't know the name of that village at the time; is that right? Somebody told you --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. We heard that. Maybe one of those people of mine, maybe they knew that that village was called Livade, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that accompanying you were two Mujahedin and a Bosnian. Apart from those persons, who else was with you?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Petko, myself, and Tosic, other than the people who were escorting us. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've answered it.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question well. Who it was, I said it was the three of us, Tosic, Maric and myself. And who was escorting us, two Mujahedin and one Bosnian, so the three of them and the three of us, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinkovic. That's clear. And when you arrived in Livade village, you mentioned that there were Mujahedin there, civilians, and you mentioned there were Bosnians. Would you agree with me that in the village, apart from the local civilians, all the others were members of the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand this quite -- the question is not clear to me. Can you please repeat it? As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: When you arrived in Livade village, you found civilians there; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say "civilians," I said civilian soldiers, these and those. Everyone was mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've explained how, when you arrived in that village, you were attacked by members of the civilian population of the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the soldiers were there. The civilians, elderly men, elderly women, were swearing at us, insulting us, "You killed my son, my child." That was the story. Someone was beating us. They would run up. And I told the story of how a soldier, a Bosnian soldier, told me to bend forward. I was bending forward as much as I could, and how this child broke my nose with his foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A Bosnian soldier of which army, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably the B and H Army. I don't know how else I could call it. Theirs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have to understand that I only completed four years of elementary school, and I am trying to speak precisely, exactly, but please just put the questions in such a way that I can understand that. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, when you refer to a Bosnian soldier, that Bosnian soldier could, in fact, have been a local Bosnian who was a member of the Mujahedin group?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, if he was a local or -- this is something that I really -- I can't tell. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you were quite clear in your evidence earlier that the men you called soldiers helped you, didn't they, they protected you from the attack from the local villagers?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that like that. What I said was that the Bosnian who was next to me and the other Mujahedin were escorting Petko and Tosic, and when they started to beat us and when that child broke my nose, then the Bosnian was telling us, "Go, go, faster, faster," as if he was trying to get us out. There was a crowd of people there. They were about to beat us more, so the Bosnian did a good job and I am grateful to him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when they got you out, they took you to a room, you mentioned, but where was it? What was the building that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was a house. The house was not demolished. There was a roof. I didn't see any damage on it, but how can I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you went into that house with your two colleagues, and you told us that you saw three other men there, Velibor Trivicevic --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Trivicevic, Sikanic, Guljevatej, and Trivicevic. There were four of them, in any case. And then the three of us arrived, so there were seven, and then by evening there was a total -- or there were a total of 12 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And while you were held in that room, you told the Court that local people, you mentioned women, came into the room and they mistreated you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you be sure how long you were actually in that room? In your evidence, you mentioned it was the second or the third day after that you left. Are you uncertain how long --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: And I stand by that. I said we were brought in the evening, so that night, then the next day, then another night, and then the -- that's how it was. On the third day, we left for Gostovici. I don't know why -- well, that's what I know. I don't know any different. I think it was two nights and two days. In any case, we spent two nights there. So two nights, let's stay with that, that we remained there for three days, two nights and three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Then you've explained to us how you were taken by a truck from Livade to another place. You were blindfolded during that journey; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the place that you've referred to as Gostovici, you didn't know -- you didn't know that that was the name of the place when you arrived there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So somebody told you that that was the name of the location?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. We just found out like that while we were there, Gostovici, like Zavidovici. That's how I remember it. That's the reason it remains lodged in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So that's not an area that you're familiar with yourself; you've never been there before?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, never, never in the area, never in Zavidovici, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us how you were put into a room in a house and given blankets; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They put blankets on the floor. The whole place had burnt down, it was charred, full of dust, and it was just for us to lie down on the floor until they got that other room ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And on your arrival, it's right, isn't it, that you were given food and water?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the next evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were at the camp, would you agree with me that you only saw both the foreign and local Mujahedin members staying at the camp?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you some questions about Gojko Vujicic.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've explained to us what happened to this man. Am I right in -- can I try and clarify when it was that he was killed? In your evidence, you said it was the first or second night. By that, did you mean it was -- this happened either the first or second night after your --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this was the second night after your arrival in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, that's the way I remember it. Whether it was the second or not, well, yes, but I do imagine it was the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's right, isn't it, that Gojko Vujicic had been seriously wounded during the attack on Krcevine? He'd been hit by a bullet in the groin; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, you were with him for some time.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that's not right. I was with Gojko that evening, when we all got together at Livade. That's when I first set eyes on him. I had no idea he'd been wounded. I hadn't known him previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, if I can refer you to a statement given by Velibor Trivicevic on the 14th of December of 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does object to the Defence leading the content of a statement that another witness gave previously. That witness will come and testify at a later date. The Prosecution does not believe that this is appropriate to confront this witness with another witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not seeking to confront this witness with another witness's testimony. I'm seeking to confront this witness with a statement made by another witness. It's like a document or piece of -- any other piece of evidence that we see in this case, and I see no reason why I shouldn't be allowed to put that statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you say? I'm looking for the appropriate Rule here which I know deals with this point, and I'm trying to remember which Rule it is. If anybody can remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the guidelines are silent as to putting statements about a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, the guidelines, but I'm thinking of a Rule. I'm not finding the Rule. In the meantime, I'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Perhaps if we can also bring it up on the screen. It's Defence exhibit -- Defence document D501. We can find that on page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S version. It's right at the very bottom of the English text. There's only two words on this page, unfortunately, but we'll scroll over. It's on the middle of the page in the B/C/S version. It's the next page in the B/C/S version. I apologise. It's the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you see the screen, Mr. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in the top paragraph, do you see the final sentence of that paragraph? On the English version, if we can scroll down to the bottom, please. Do you see there, Mr. Marinkovic, where it says: "Two men were wounded. Stokanovic had been shot in the lower right leg, and Vujicic was hit by a bullet in the groin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can go over into the English so it's -- if we can -- Your Honours, you can see that "two men" appears on the English version. If we can scroll over to the English so you can see the remainder of the sentence. So if we can turn to page 7 in the English, please. It says: "Two men were wounded. Stokanovic had been shot in the lower right leg and Vujicic was hit by a bullet in the groin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say whose statement is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is the statement of Velibor Trivicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Marinkovic, Velibor Trivicevic was somebody who was with you during the camp, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: He's somebody that you know?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes; not just him, all 11 of them, those who are still alive. Well, Gojko, Gojko is no longer among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So where he says that Gojko Vujicic had been hit by a bullet in the groin, do you have any comment on that? Do you agree? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As for Stokanovic, yes, but not about Gojko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You've explained how, on the evening that Mr. Vujicic died, he'd been calling out, he'd been asking for water. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that he was cursing, he was calling out curse words?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that he cursed God, he referred to God?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it was at that point that you heard the rifle shot?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'll explain that. Everything is correct but this: Gojko asked for water. We all were asking for water. And he said, "Give me some water to drink. Fuck the sun and every planet. Get me some water to drink, and then you might as well finish me off." And then the Bosnian was off to fetch us some water and brought back urine, and then they were telling me, "That's not right, the bullet right away, immediately, no." But that's our assumption, because the Mujahedin had told us when we had been captured, he translated this into English, and this Samac knew some English and then he translated it for us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But you'll agree with me -- well, earlier on you had agreed with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remind, for the French, that the translation into French is about 30 seconds, even a minute later, after the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just go back to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that the French interpreters has just said what I already knew, actually; that is to say that they do not translate from B/C/S, they interpret from English. Therefore, first you have the B/C/S, then after the English interpretation, and finally only the French interpretation. I would like to remind everybody of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I didn't know that. Two points I just wanted to raise with you. The witness had said -- the interpreter said he didn't hear what the witness said, and the guidelines on that point you were raising are not silent, actually. If you look at paragraph 4 and paragraph 11. But you can do that in your spare time. All I want to say is that they forbid you telling the witness the name of the witness whose statement you are putting to him. And I think you have told him already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I'll take that on board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, if we could go back to what you were just telling us, because the interpreter didn't catch the last part of your answer. Could you explain again what the Mujahedin said when he heard Gojko Vujicic cursing?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not about what the Mujahedin said. How should I know what he said, the Mujahedin? Maybe he was saying some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please be asked to remove his hand from his mouth, because we can't hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, please, could you remove your hand from your mouth? The interpreters are asking you to do so. Thank you, thank you. Just so I can clarify this before I move on: You agreed with me earlier that Gojko Vujicic had been cursing God; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The sun. He was cursing the sun, God, no matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then at some stage later, after he'd done so, there was the rifle shot, and you learned that he'd been killed?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not right away. No, no, no, not right. The shot -- first he asked for water and this and that, and sometime later a rifle fired. We had no idea what had happened. And then he never showed up again. We didn't know what had occurred until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, thank you. So that happened on the second night that you were in the camp. What I'd like to ask you about is: After that event took place, do you remember a tall Mujahedin coming and visiting you and the other men in your room?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they came. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that he told you that you would not be subjected to any more beatings, but you all had to avoid swearing?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not quite what I said. We were captured and taken there, and then this Mujahedin came. I never said he was tall. Was he tall, was he not tall? He was quite stout, barely. He said this in English, and then Miodrag Samac told us what he had said, "No swearing, no F word. As soon as one of you utters the F word, heads will be rolling." I don't know if he said that or not. That's what we were told. This man just came over. He was big, Mujahedin. Yeah, Mujahedin, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me from that point onwards, after that Mujahedin had visited you, there was a turning point and your treatment at the camp improved?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It never really improved, if I may. If not, not -- roughly speaking, but it's just my take on it, there was the camp, and then they went to the front line -- or came back from the front line. We would hear them coming back. This would normally be about half past 2.00. A Mujahedin cried out -- I don't know what they said, and then everybody went, "Allah Ekber." It was like a whole platoon of them coming back from somewhere, and then they would take us all out, all of us Chetniks, as they said, to have a look at us, and then they would round us up, line us up. They would spit at us. We were literally dripping with their drivel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a statement of another witness who was there. I'm not going to reveal the identity. But I would like the Court's permission to put that statement -- refer to that statement to this witness. I'm not sure what sense the witness will make of it, though, if I'm not permitted to reveal the identity of the maker of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know. What has the statement got to do with the name or what has the name got to do with the content?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can front this witness with the statement of the other witness who was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can confront him with a statement without mentioning the name. The guidelines specifically say don't mention the name. But before you do that, what do you want us to do with D449?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not proposing to admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, let me put to you the statement made by one of the other men who was with you in the camp. What he says is that: "During our stay in the Kamenica camp, there was a kind of turning point regarding our treatment on the 26th of July, 1995. On that day, we were given the opportunity to take a shower." So, Mr. Marinkovic, one of the men with you has said that on the 26th of July, only a short while after you arrived there, there was a turning point in the treatment and you were permitted to take showers. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not true. May I explain what it was like concerning showers. I don't know what that witness said. Ask him. If you ask me about these showers, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, you obviously don't agree with that witness. Would you agree with me that you were given food and water each day after the incident involving Mr. Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We were given breakfast and dinner every day. We sometimes got green cabbage, and then sometimes some canned food, but there were no spoons, so we got some bread, each of us a little. And when the sediment came up, we would scoop that up with our hands. As for showers, if you want me to, I can tell you about that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Marinkovic: It's right as well that following the incident involving Mr. Vujicic, Dr. Sikanic was given medical supplies so he could treat the injuries of the men in the room, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: There's some truth to that. That was several days later. Stokanovic had a wound just below his knee, and Petko and the other guy had wire marks on their hand. That was several days later. This began to stink, and then they threw something into a sack, some bandages, something. There were no other medicines, just some bandages to dress wounds, of course, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that Vinko Aksentic, one of the other men, had a wound on his hand, and Dr. Sikanic was able to treat that as well?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't just Vinko Aksentic, it was Petko too. They had wounds from the wire. They had had their tendons sliced. Those were wounds. It wasn't just Stokanovic. There were two or three people with those wounds. But it's not much of a question. If he had been in a position to treat anyone, he probably would have treated everyone alike.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, the interpreter did not understand the last part of your answer. Could you just repeat the last part? You said that he probably would have treated everyone alike.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, right. Most probably, Vinko, wounds on his hands, but not just Vinko. Petko, Vinko and Stokan [phoen], they all had wounds, so he wouldn't simply have treated Vinko without treating the other two as well. That's what I said. He would have treated all three of them. He dressed their wounds, all three of them, yes, that's true, but it's not like he discriminated between them. It's just that he couldn't, he couldn't at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right to say, isn't it, that just before you left the camp and travelled to Zenica, in the day or so before, a Mujahedin came who was a doctor, and he worked with Dr. Sikanic to give treatment to the men in the room?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I know someone brought that, a Mujahedin or a Bosnian, some nylon that evening, chucked it inside, "Doctor, Doctor," talked to him, "Right, all right, fair enough."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, it's the case, isn't it, that the Mujahedin doctor worked with Dr. Sikanic to prepare bandages, and Dr. Sikanic prepared -- treated the men?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. Someone may have, but I didn't, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have many more questions, but I think this would be a convenient time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, you told us how you were transported from the camp to Zenica. At the time that you were transported, were there any visible signs of mistreatment on either you or the other men who had been at the camp?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that I had traces of -- or signs of mistreatment. As for the others, they bore the signs of what was in the camp from wire and other things. But I did have visible signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in is whether there were any visible signs, say, on your face or perhaps hands.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Not on the face. On the legs, yes, but I did have the signs on my face where -- after I was hit by the soldier, by the rifle-butt, where the tooth broke through. And on the head, I explained. And then on the leg, I have still to this very day an open wound. That was from when they had to break the padlock with the hammer to release my legs from the bindings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear about that, you say that you had a sign of an injury on your face, but concerning the other men, you can't say whether or not they had?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. I saw the marks from the wire on Petko, Stokanovic and on Vinko, what I saw. As for other signs, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to have a look at a document now. It's P2471. Can you read the heading of that document, Mr. Marinkovic? Can you see what it says? Would you agree with me this is a document dated the 28th of August, 1995, and it has the heading "Official Note"?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I don't expect you to have seen this document before, but if you look at the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- can you see that this is an official note that was compiled on the 28th of August, 1995, with you, Krstan Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I don't see it all that well. It's too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's not a very clear copy. Perhaps a hard copy could be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we could scroll down the English, please, and let's read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you make out the paper copy of the document I've given to you, Mr. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It's small, but, yes, I will try. Can I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: There's no need to read it out loud, but would you agree with me that in the note, what we can see is information that you provided to the person who interviewed you --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here "Krstan Marinkovic." I don't know who the person it's -- you have to tell me. I'm really finding it difficult to find my way around here. All I know is "Krstan Marinkovic." But as for the person that I'm supposed to be meeting with, then that, you have to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, let's just see what information is recorded here. It says: "Compiled on 28th of August following an interview with Krstan Marinkovic." It then gives some details: "Son of Petar and Mladja." Are they your parents' names?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It gives a date of birth, the 18th of January, 1947. Is that your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Eighteenth of January, 1947, is my date of birth. That's the way -- and what it says here, the 18th of January, yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then we can say -- we can see there are more details. It says that Marinkovic is married, the father of one, a farmer by occupation who --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: "Completed four grades of primary school."

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: "Permanently residing in Crkvena village"?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you happy that this document is talking about you?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that when -- once you arrived in KP Dom in Zenica, you were interviewed by a member -- members of the Bosnian Army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look further down the note, would you agree with me that here you provide information about your father, Petar, your wife, your daughter, you give information about the --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see there's information about your daughter's husband; is that so?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we move down through the document on to page 2 in the English version, we can see there that you continue to talk about your family, and then you talk about a very rich Croat, Petar Sombrski, a person who had brought Muslims to work in his fields.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not correct that I said that. That is not correct. Go ahead, and I will tell you whether it is or not, but this is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't think we need to dwell too long on that piece of information, but you would agree with me that in the document, you then go on to explain to the interviewer about how you were assigned to your platoon, and you give military information about your unit; is that so, Mr. Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, this is not correct. It's not correct that Petar Sombrski brought Muslims to work at his place. I said that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has the witness accepted that this is information provided by him or this is just information from this document? I keep hearing you saying, "You provided this," "You said this to the interviewer."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, from what you've seen from the document, and please feel free to look through it further, if necessary, there's a lot of detailed information in that document about you and your family members. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree that he asked me who I had, brothers, Radivoje, father, mother, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you would agree that in this document, we can see that somebody has recorded information about your family, your father, mother, daughters, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, would you -- well, you have the document in front of you. It's true, isn't it, that the document contains information about -- detailed information about your family members; you agree?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that the reason that the person that prepared this document was able to write down that detailed information about you and your family members was because you provided that information to him?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me that I don't know that. I mean, who could that be? It's probably the person that I provided it to did that. Everything else -- everything about my family and everything is correct, but what it says about Petar Sombrski, that is something that is incorrect. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You agree that you were interviewed whilst you were detained in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that when you were interviewed, the person interviewing you, or persons interviewing you, made a note of the information you provided?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: How can I know what they were doing? How could I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps you could know that because now, in front of us, there is a document containing very detailed information that says that an interview took place on the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Cannot know what date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a specific part of this document. If we can turn to page 3 in the English version, I'll just try and ascertain what it is in the B/C/S version. Mr. Marinkovic, if you could take the document in front of you -- I apologise for this, Your Honour. This is our only copy. Could the usher please return it to us? I think that will be the quickest way to deal with this point. We've located it. If the document could please be returned to the witness. And in the English version on page 3, it's the text -- it's just below the halfway section, and it concerns the Mujahedin. Mr. Marinkovic, could you just read that last page to yourself and try and identify the section that talks about the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not particularly proficient at reading, anyway, but I'll just take it slowly and see how far I get. Am I supposed to read this out loud or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you can read it, you can read it out. What I'm interested in is the -- it's the part that begins: "In his statement, the interviewed person said he did not know that they had been attacked by the Mujahedin." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement -- ah, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should read it to you, Mr. Marinkovic. It says --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: "In his statement, the interviewed person said he did not know that they had been attacked by the Mujahedin. Otherwise, he would have not surrendered, because they were told, after the 27 May 1995 operation that the Mujahedin have no mercy and that they kill, do not take prisoners. He said that the survivors of the operation told him harrowing stories, but he says that he sees that he was lucky and the stories are not completely true." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I find this a little unclear. It is like not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question? Do you see the section in your text that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I did see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, then, that what you told the interviewer on that day was, in effect, that you'd heard bad things about the Mujahedin, but the reality was that the Mujahedin were not so bad as you had been led to believe? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not true. I have nothing to do with this. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me -- you've just read the section relating to the Mujahedin, you've had a chance to look at this document. There is no other information about the Mujahedin in this document, is there?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't read this, to begin with. I don't know, but I'm listening to you and your questions, and I can only tell you that I don't quite understand this and I don't understand this question. About me hearing bad words and this not being that way, I didn't say that. That was added. I don't know. Nor did I provide this sort of information anywhere ever, what the Mujahedin were like, nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: But you would agree with me or you would take it from me that this is the only reference to the Mujahedin in this document in which you've provided detailed -- detailed information has been provided about you and your family?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this document, and I've got nothing to do with it, believe me. I don't remember this. I don't know that anyone ever asked me that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinkovic. The final point, if I may, you'll recall earlier on today you were shown three photographs showing damaged houses. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that what we saw in those photographs, those types of houses, damaged, with two chimneys, were a common sight in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You could see those sort of houses in many different places?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Marinkovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I sit down, please, could that last document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document P2471 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, could you tell us how the Bosnian soldier, the one you called a Bosnian soldier when you were captured, the one that was with the two others which you called the two Mujahedins, so could you tell us how the Bosnian soldier was dressed, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't. I didn't look closely. All three of them wore uniforms, the camouflage uniform, the olive drab one, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But all three were dressed in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the soldiers who were going in and out, off and on, in the house where you were in Gostovici; do you remember how those soldiers were dressed, the ones you called Bosnian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian soldiers wore camouflage uniforms. The Mujahedin, I don't know what they wear when they go into action. But when they were there, they would drape themselves in something and wear slippers and something, I don't know, like a skirt or something. It certainly was no uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marinkovic. This case, as you will understand, has to do with the activities of the Mujahedin, and so I have a question regarding some of the activities which you have not testified about. My question is: Do you recall if the Mujahedin came to register you when you had been taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't recall or does it mean that you know for sure that you were not registered?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Either we weren't registered or I don't remember. But as far as I know, we were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Proper registration would have been if someone had come to you and asked for your name and your rank, and the --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Bosnians then, not the Mujahedin. How could we possibly have understood them, how? If he, for example, asked me -- no, no, I don't remember that. Maybe in the presence of a Bosnian, but the Mujahedin, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Fair enough. So a Bosnian soldier then came to register you, is that -- but do you recall giving your name and your date of birth and your rank to anybody after you'd been taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably, we had to be listed, but I think it was the Bosnians who did that. How could we possibly have communicated with the Mujahedin? There had to be some sort of a list, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. When you were then transferred from the Kamenica camp to Zenica, were you then in some way exchanged later on with other prisoners or ...

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I left on the 23rd, 24th of August for Zenica, and I left Zenica on the 25th. On the 25th, I arrived home, December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you sat for four months or so in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose. The front line, Gostovici, Zenica. A total of just under six months, I believe. Actually, I left home on the 30th of June, and I was back home on the 25th of December, 1995. Five days under six months, according to my simple calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: After the war had ended, you were released.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The 21st of November, at Zenica, there was a "tanoj" [phoen] and it was announced over the "tanoj" that the Dayton Accord had been signed, so we knew about that. But again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the aspect that I'm interested in, if you know, that is, how the transfer from the Kamenica camp was arranged to Zenica. You were held by the Mujahedin in the Kamenica camp, and then you were transferred to the Bosnian Army's detention centre in Zenica. Do you know how this transfer was made, how it was arranged?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that, didn't I, but I'll repeat. On the 24th, the afternoon of the 24th at Gostovici, we were taken out and chained. Someone blindfolded us. And then from there, we got to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand how it happened, but what I'm asking is if you know the arrangements that were made between the El Mujahid Detachment and the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know about that, no, no. I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Except --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. I just wish to express our compassion with the suffering that you have endured. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, just a few questions. When you were in the trench on the 21st of July, 1995, against which army were your units fighting?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, either. Most probably -- I don't know. I find the question unclear. I was on one side, then most probably that belongs to the Serb Republic, and these other guys, the Federation or something. Which army was there? I do know that. The Bosnian Army and the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It was the Bosnian Army and the Mujahedin that was there. Okay, thank you very much. You may find the next one perhaps still unclear. You've talked about soldiers being in uniform when you were somewhere in a house. Do you know which army those uniforms belonged to? Of which army were those uniforms, if you do know?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: You know something, it was difficult to tell uniforms at the time. Was it olive drab, as back in Tito's time, the camouflage? The one or the other. Who on earth could have known what belonged to who. No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say you don't know. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You kept on saying, during cross-examination by Mr. Robson, that, "If you want me to tell you about showers, I can tell you." I would like to hear about showers.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Say, for example, the story about washing up, we were in a chain from Gostovici down a road, across that road, went down a riverbank, crossed some river. I think it was called -- I'm not sure what. I used to know what it was called. It's full of pebbles and stones, large stones. It's not very deep. Line us up next to the river, and then face down into the water, chained up. We go back, we dry up. It takes us until next Thursday to dry. We have chains on our feet. And we were like that all the way to Zenica. Every time we went to that river to wash, we always had to dry like that, no changing clothes, no nothing. So much for the showers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Finally, and that is if you so wish, and if you don't wish, I'm quite prepared to back off, would you be prepared to show us the wound on your foot?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: How will I do that? Can you see it? Do I take a photo of it and leave a photo behind when I leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions on the questions -- arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just one question arising from some of the questions put by Judge Harhoff. I think the record might be a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: At page 74, line 2, and again at line 9, Mr. Marinkovic, you say: "It was the Bosnians who came to register us. If we were registered, it was the Bosnians who did it." I just want to make clear, from that answer -- it might not be that clear. Were you, in fact, ever registered during your --

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no way I can know, before Zenica. Perhaps we were. But I know about when we got to Zenica, the evening we arrived, one by one, into the office. I didn't even say, "Good evening." There was a man at the door, "Good evening, good evening," all right, then going back, "Good evening," listed, registered. And over there, I don't know. It's possible, but I don't know for sure. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That's the only question I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just one issue, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Robson:

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, in response to Judge Lattanzi's question when she asked you about soldiers going in and out of the house, you said the Bosnian soldiers -- that the Bosnian soldiers wore camouflage uniform. Now, as I understand -- as I understood your evidence earlier on, you didn't really have the opportunity to look at these Bosnian -- these men you call Bosnian soldiers in any detail, did you?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: You're not right. We had to keep our heads down, but then the Bosnians were right next to us. For example, their military boots, they would step on everyone's toes with those boots. Well, I do see the trousers and uniform, don't I, stepping on everyone's toes, saying, "Anyone for a punch-up with me?" Well, of course, I stole a glimpse now and then. I wasn't supposed to, of course, but I did all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And these men you've referred to as soldiers were wearing different types of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You had to keep your head down?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You didn't see any insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: KRSTAN MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't, because then you have to look up. But still there's this man standing right next to you, you keep your head down, you see him to some extent. But if you look up, no, no, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marinkovic, this concludes your testimony, and we take the time to say thank you to you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused, and you may stand down. But before you do so, we just want to express our hope that your wound does heal finally. I know it's been a long time, but let's hope it does for you. You may now stand down. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps before the witness leaves, if he could be cautioned. There's a possibility that another witness might be staying at the same hotel with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I don't know whether you do know the next witness that is going to be called and whether you stayed in the same hotel. We caution you to please not discuss this case with that witness. Yes, Madam Vidovic. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand. I understand my colleague's concern, but we remain adamant that this witness not stay at the same hotel. It's totally meaningless -- it's pointless to keep them both at the same hotel, risking the possibility that they might, in fact, discuss the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be allowed to ask the Chamber a single question? May I? Say, for example, this man was with me at the camp from day one, we're together there, right, how could I possibly affect him, how could he possibly affect me? We spent those six months together. I don't see what difference it makes. There is absolutely no logic to this. This is an educated person. I'm, you know, salt of the earth, four grades of elementary school. But there is absolutely no need for me. I don't get it. But if it's a problem, well, I can understand that, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We understand what you are saying. All we're saying is, from your side, if you can keep your side of the bargain and not talk to him. And while you are there, Madam Vidovic, the question of the same hotel was raised by me for the first time, and I said, if I may quote myself, "I don't know whether you do know the next witness that is going to be called and whether you stay in the same hotel." I don't know whether they do, ma'am, and unfortunately the arrangements of where witnesses stay is beyond this Chamber. I have not been able to -- I don't know how I can come to your rescue there, except from what I've just said to the witness. I don't know whether they stay in the same hotel. They may not be staying in the same hotel. So thank you very much, Mr. Marinkovic. You may stand down. And have a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution does not have any further witnesses for today. The witness scheduled to appear tomorrow will be made available tomorrow, and we anticipate that his evidence will take one full day and that we will be able to complete his evidence during the course of the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. Court adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom. Court adjourned. Sorry, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just raise two issues. The first issue, perhaps I can deal with briefly. There's no disrespect meant to the Bench, but the Defence just wishes to raise a slight concern about the way in which compassion is expressed to the witness. We appreciate, of course, that we're dealing with an emotive subject today, and obviously the witness spoke powerful evidence, but it could be said there may be a perception that perhaps the Bench -- I'm sure there isn't, but there could be said that there is a conception that the Bench has somehow pre -- made a pre-judgement as to the credibility of the witness. I'm not saying that you have, but the perception may be there, and hence we're just raising that. We feel it's our duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was the one who expressed the compassion, and I did it upon careful consideration, because I believe that in all cases, not only this trial but in all of the trials here, the witnesses who have also become -- or who were also victims are, in most cases, showing enormous efforts to come here and tell their stories again. It is a very exhausting and a huge sacrifice for most of them, and I feel that if the Tribunal doesn't in some way express some sort of feeling about what they have been through and acknowledge the courage they had to come and testify, then I think that the Tribunal would not be meeting its task in a satisfactory way altogether. I find that it is really important for the Bench to show, not only in this trial but in all the trials, that we see the pain that they have been through, we feel compassion with them, and this, in my view, does not in any way express any sort of prejudicial attitude. It is simply meant out of respect from one man to another that I realise that he has been through a lot of pain and he has taken the courage to come and explain this to me. This is a very ethical issue, and I think not only that I will do it but I should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly no criticism is intended. I'm talking a perception. I'm not suggesting that the Bench has in any way, shape, or form made any pre-judgement, and I do appreciate the explanation that you've given, which certainly has set out your reasons in saying what you did to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to -- I also want to assert myself, because I also said something along those lines. I asked him to show his wound and I wished him recovery. But I just want to say, in addition to what Judge Harhoff has said, the fact of injuries is not a disputed fact in this case, is it? You didn't dispute it, you didn't dispute that he was injured. All you're saying is the accused is not to blame for that. That's what you are saying. I haven't heard this to be a disputed thing, so I'm not quite sure how pre-judging, even as a perception, begins to enter the picture. However, I understand that that's your view, and I just want to say that it was a comment on an issue that is not disputed and it is said in the light of what Judge Harhoff has said, just like when the accused takes the witness stand or anybody takes the witness stand for the Defence, we've got to show that respect to them. We've got to show that compassion to both sides, and if any Defence witness comes in here and says, "They shot me," or what have you, the opposite side, we've got to show that compassion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and I'm grateful for the explanation that's been given. I wonder, however, if I could raise a second point. Again, I'll do so quickly. It comes back to a procedural matter that arose during the course of the cross-examination, the issue of putting witness statements made by another witness to the witness who's testifying. Your Honours, I've checked the guidelines, and it would appear to me that paragraph 4 -- paragraph 11 of the guidelines relates specifically to a situation where a party put witness testimony given by another witness in either the same case or a different case to the witness who's testifying in court and not witness statements. The point that I would make is that if you have a person who sets down in writing their point of view on a particular issue, if they put it in a letter, then that letter could be shown to the witness without any problems. It would be the same thing if they wrote it down in a diary. That diary could be presented to the witness who's testifying in court without any difficulties. However, because the witness has sat with an OTP investigator and they have put down that witness's statement onto a piece of paper, somehow it seems that what we've discussed today, that would prevent that witness statement being put to the other testifying witness, and in my submission that somehow doesn't quite make sense. In the case of where a witness has sat down with an OTP investigator, they've done so having been warned of the risks of perjury and that there could be serious consequences for not telling the truth, so in essence I would suggest that an OTP witness statement could be more valuable than something that's been reduced into writing in a letter, or a diary, or any other type of document. So based on the guidelines and based on what I've just mentioned, in my submission, Your Honours, I'd hoped that we would be able to put the witness statements of other witnesses to a witness who's testifying before us in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's read the part out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The parties are requested to avoid interpreting or paraphrasing what a witness has previously either stated or testified. The Trial Chamber considered that such interpreting of paraphrasing increases the risk of mis-characterising the prior statement or testimony. So it does deal with both, both statement and testimony. I thought you said -- in the beginning, you said that paragraph 4 and 11 do not deal with statement, they deal with testimony only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand paragraph 4, it's dealing with misinterpretation or mis-paraphrasing what's contained in a statement or testimony. Therefore, I absolutely agree that if a witness statement is put to a witness who's testifying, it should state exactly what's written on the paper. It shouldn't mischaracterise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Paragraph 11 regulates that "don't tell him who this witness statement -- who the author of the other statement is."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The difference with paragraph 11, Your Honour, with respect, is that it only talks about testimony, so we would say that we would draw a distinction between a witness statement and testimony. Paragraph 11 contains the prohibition on confronting a witness with the testimony of another witness. It's silent as to a witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I throw in something here? It was actually Judge Lattanzi who drew my attention to it, and maybe she should take the floor here, but to show a witness who has testified already and will no longer testify here what other witnesses have testified is probably permissible, but it is complicated, to say the least, to show a witness who is currently testifying what other witnesses who will be called are going to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the -- with respect to one of the witness statements that I was seeking to confront this witness with, it was indeed a witness who will testify in the near future. But putting that to one side, with the other statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is he a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, no. He's a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are not certain whether he may testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, he may not, indeed, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just sorry to interrupt, but for purpose of clarification, with respect to Witness Trivicevic, he's testifying tomorrow. That's tomorrow's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. But for purposes of the discussion, a witness who has yet to testify, you may not testify -- even now you might decide to withdraw him. That's all we are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In respect of one of the other witness statements that I was seeking to confront the witness with, he's not a witness in this case. What I would also add is that I've spoken to other Defence counsel on other cases about this particular issue, and it seems there is a split practice in the Tribunal. And what I can tell you is that from my -- from speaking to Defence counsel in the Haradinaj case and the Boskoski case, in respect of those cases, certainly witness statements made by other witnesses who may or may not testify in the case are put to witnesses who are currently testifying in court as a matter of course. It happens with great regularity. So essentially all I'm really inviting the Trial Chamber to do is really follow the practice that many of the -- well, that other Trial Chambers follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure whether we are bound by the practice of other Trial Chambers. Maybe parties might want to prepare submissions on the point, and we'll look at them and may decide whether or not to amend the guidelines. Wouldn't that be a neater way of dealing with the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd certainly be happy to take that course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's leave it on that basis. Thank you very much. Any other matter? Thank you very much. Then that brings us to the end of the day. We'll adjourn until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
